modern: Do not despise death, but be well content with it, since this too is one of those things which nature wills. For just as it is to be young and to grow old, and to grow and to reach maturity, and to have teeth and beard and grey hairs, and to father children and to be pregnant and to give birth, and all the other natural processes which the seasons of your life bring, so too is dissolution. This, then, is in keeping with the character of a thoughtful man—to be neither careless nor impatient nor contemptuous with regard to death, but to wait for it as one of the processes of nature. As you now wait for the time when the child shall come out of your wife’s womb, so be ready for the time when your soul shall fall out of this covering. But if you also want a common kind of comfort which will reach your heart, you will be best reconciled to death by observing the things from which you are going to be removed, and the morals of those with whom your soul will no longer be mingled. For it is in no way right to be offended with men, but it is your duty to care for them and to bear with them gently; and yet to remember that your departure will not be from men who have the same principles as yourself. For this is the only thing, if there is any, which could pull us the other way and attach us to life—to be allowed to live with those who have the same principles as ourselves. But as it is, you see how great is the trouble arising from the discord of those who live together, so that you may say: Come quickly, O death, in case I too should forget myself.

As thou now waitest for the time when the child shall come out of thy wife’s womb, so be ready for the time when thy soul shall fall out of this envelope. But if thou requirest also a vulgar kind of comfort which shall reach thy heart, thou wilt be made best reconciled to death by observing the objects from which thou art going to be removed, and the morals of those with whom thy soul will no longer be mingled. For it is no way right to be offended with men, but it is thy duty to care for them and to bear with them gently; and yet to remember that thy departure will not be from men who have the same principles as thyself. For this is the only thing, if there be any, which could draw us the contrary way and attach us to life,—to be permitted to live with those who have the same principles as ourselves.
